lines.text: A question you type into ChatGPT on your phone sets off billions of multiplications on a chip in a data centre, far from you.
That chip sends the answer back in small pieces, and every single piece takes the whole trip through the model.
Here is the whole trip. Your words get cut into tokens, the tokens turn into numbers, and the numbers climb through the model's layers.
A chip does the multiplying, one next word comes out, and then the whole trip starts again for the word after it.
We'll follow GPT-three, an earlier model that OpenAI described in a research paper, with 175B parameters. Newer chatbots are built on the same idea.
First stop: what does the model actually read? Not letters, and not quite words either.
Your question is cut into tokens: common chunks of text, like a whole short word, or a piece of a longer one.
In English, a token is about 4 characters long on average, according to OpenAI.
OpenAI also puts one token at roughly 75% of an English word, so a long answer can run to hundreds of tokens.
Why chunks, and not whole words? A common word is often a single token, while a rare word or a name gets cut into several pieces, so any word can still be built from pieces on the list.
The cutting follows a fixed list of chunks that was settled before the model was trained, so the same text is always cut the same way.
Every chunk on that list has its own ID number, and that number is all the model is handed for each token.
But an ID is only a label. It says nothing about what the word means. So how does a label become meaning?
Next stop: the model looks each ID up in a giant table and pulls out a long list of numbers for that token.
So who chose those numbers? Nobody, by hand. Training set them, nudging each one a tiny bit at a time across enormous amounts of text.
Each list works like a point in a space with thousands of directions, and tokens used in similar ways end up close together.
Cat lands near dog. Paris lands near London. Nobody placed them there; training did.
And how does it know which word came first? Each token also gets a second list added, marking its place in the sentence, because the order of words changes what they mean.
Now your question is a row of number lists. What happens to them next is where almost all the work is done.
Next stop, the layers. Why does a model need so many of them?
GPT-three stacks dozens of these layers, one on top of the next, and the row of number lists passes through every single one, in order.
On a single floor, what comes first? Every token looks back at the tokens before it, and takes in a little of what they carry.
That is how blue in your question can take on the meaning of a colour, not a mood, from the words around it.
Then each token's list goes through a block of multiplications on its own, and its numbers come out slightly changed.
Floor after floor, the lists change a little each time. By the top, a list no longer stands for one word. It carries what the whole sentence is about.
The multiplying on every floor uses numbers stored inside the model, called parameters. And that is where size comes in.
Because those parameters have to be multiplied somewhere, by something you can touch. That is where the software meets the hardware.
So where does all this multiplying actually happen? In a data centre, on racks of servers packed with graphics chips.
GPT-three has 175B parameters, and every one of them is used in a multiplication for every single token it writes.
Those numbers are the model. There is no list of facts inside it, only parameters, set during training.
Inside the chip, what does the work? Thousands of tiny maths units. Each one multiplies two numbers and adds the result to a running total.
They all work at once, so a whole grid of numbers is multiplied in one sweep, and a chip like this does hundreds of trillions of them every second.
Where do the parameters wait? In memory stacked right beside the chip, and they stream into those maths units over and over, token after token.
A model this big is usually split across several chips, passing numbers back and forth between them over fast links.
All that switching turns into heat, which is why data centres need so much power, and so much cooling.
So far: words became tokens, tokens became numbers, the numbers climbed the layers, and a chip did the maths. And all of that makes just one token.
One token? Out of everything it could say, how does it choose?
The top layer gives a score to every token on the list, tens of thousands of them, for how well each would fit next.
For the first word of an answer about the blue sky, tokens like Sunlight or Because score high, and banana scores almost nothing.
Then one token is picked, usually one of the likely ones, with a little randomness, which is why the same question can get a different answer.
That token is added to the end of the text, and the model reads your question plus the new token, and makes the whole trip again.
Up through every layer, once more, just to pick the token after that. Then again. And again.
That is why you see the answer appear piece by piece. You are watching it being written, one token at a time.
Doesn't that waste time? To save it, the chip keeps notes about the earlier tokens in its memory, so it doesn't redo all of their maths from the beginning.
It ends when the token it picks is a special one that means stop.
So does it look your answer up? Not on its own. Unless the app gives it a search tool, it predicts each next token from patterns it learned.
That is why it can sound sure and still be wrong. A likely-sounding token isn't always a true one.
But there is a limit to how much text it can look back on while it writes. And GPT-three's limit was small.
GPT-three could read only a limited number of tokens at once, called its window. It held your question, everything said before it, and the answer so far.
At about 4 characters a token, that window held only a few pages of text, not a whole book.
And what happens to anything older? It drops out of the window. The model simply can't see it any more, as if it was never said.
It doesn't remember you between chats either, unless the app copies your earlier messages back into the window.
Newer models have far bigger windows, but the rule is the same: if it isn't in the window, the model doesn't see it.
Now follow it back out. The picked token leaves the chip, crosses the data centre, and travels the network to your phone.
On your screen it lands as a few letters. Then the next one arrives, and the next, faster than you can read.
So in GPT-three, every token of an answer is a fresh vote among tens of thousands of tokens, cast by 175B numbers, multiplied on a chip.
Which step should we take apart next? Tell us. And next time you type a question, watch the first word arrive.
